pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 5–7 (high centrality — the iconic-animals hub); name and recognise iconic rainforest animals — jaguars, toucans, sloths, poison dart frogs, howler monkeys, macaws and butterflies — AND know which layer of the rainforest each lives in.
• Standards—UK: DfE KS1 Y1 'Animals, including humans' (identify/name/group animals) and Y2 'Living things and their habitats' (living things in their habitat).
• Standards—US: NGSS 1-LS1-1 (external parts help survival); 2-LS4-1 (diversity of life); K-ESS3-1.
• Operational details: pair naming with PLACING — each iconic animal to its rainforest layer, using the four-layer map from the previous topic (jaguar on the floor, howler monkeys/toucans/macaws/sloths in the canopy, butterflies flitting between, dart frogs low and damp). This turns a field-guide list into an ecological where-they-live picture. Give each animal one memorable feature/hook (sloth = slow, howler = loudest, dart frog = tiny and bright). Reinforce that the busy canopy holds most of them.
• Checkpoint: Tier A (5) name three iconic rainforest animals; Tier B (6) place one animal in its layer (e.g. monkeys in the canopy); Tier C (7) explain that different animals live in different layers, with most in the canopy.
bestPractices: Always place each animal in its LAYER, reusing the four-layer map, so naming becomes ecological understanding
Give each animal a single sticky hook (sloth = slowest, howler = loudest, jaguar = big cat of the floor)
Use real photos/calls so recognition is vivid and the noisy canopy comes alive
Reinforce that most animals live in the sunny canopy, echoing the layers topic
Sort animals to layers as a game to check the naming-plus-placing goal
keyRepresentations: Layered forest scene with each iconic animal shown in its home layer
Animal cards (name + one hook + its layer)
Canopy close-up crowded with monkeys, toucans, macaws and sloths
commonMisconceptions: All rainforest animals live on the ground — most live up in the canopy
Every animal lives everywhere in the forest — different animals favour different layers
Sloths are fast/monkeys — sloths are very slow and are not monkeys
Poison dart frogs are big and dangerous to touch randomly — they are tiny; their bright colour is a warning
Jaguars live in trees all the time — they mainly prowl the forest floor

learn.summary: For ages 5–7, children name and recognise iconic Neotropical rainforest animals (jaguars, toucans, sloths, poison dart frogs, howler monkeys, macaws, butterflies) AND place each in its rainforest layer, reusing the four-layer map so naming becomes ecological understanding. Each animal gets one sticky hook (sloth = slowest, howler = loudest, jaguar = big cat of the floor). The central idea: most animal life is in the sunny canopy, and different animals favour different layers because of how they move and where their food is — while a few mobile animals (like butterflies) move between layers.

activities.title: Explore the layered forest alive with animals
feedback: When an animal is selected, reveal its name, its one-line hook, and highlight the layer it lives in so recognition and placement happen together.
For the butterfly, reveal that it moves between layers (e.g. canopy and understorey) rather than lighting a single fixed layer, matching its mobility.
OPTIONAL: play the howler monkey's roar when its animal is chosen so the noisy canopy comes alive; use real photos/calls to make recognition vivid.
For 'Which layer has the MOST animals?', confirm by lighting up the crowded canopy, reinforcing that most life is in the sunny roof.
activities.rationale: Pairing naming with placing turns a field-guide list into an ecological where-they-live picture at the right 5–7 grain. A highlight linking each animal to its layer makes the naming-plus-placing goal concrete, while treating mobile species like butterflies as moving between layers keeps it accurate. Optional sound and real photos may make recognition vivid. This is a proposed scaffold, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Iconic Neotropical rainforest animals (jaguars, toucans, sloths, poison dart frogs, howler monkeys, macaws, butterflies) occupy characteristic forest layers, with most animal life in the canopy
KS1 pupils identify, name and group animals and describe how habitats provide for them
learnerActions: Revisit the tall four-layer forest scene (floor, understorey/low damp, canopy, emergent/above) from the layers topic, now populated with iconic animals.

Explore each animal to find out its name, a memorable hook, and which layer it calls home: jaguar padding across the shadowy floor ('big cat, hunts on the ground'); a howler monkey in the canopy ('loudest animal here — lives in the sunny roof'); a sloth ('slowest of all, hangs in the canopy'); a toucan and macaws in the canopy; a tiny bright poison dart frog low in the damp; drifting butterflies that move between layers.
Answer a lift-the-flap style question: 'Which layer has the MOST animals?' and see the crowded canopy highlighted.
activities.intendedInsight: The rainforest isn't just full of creatures — most animals have a home layer, and the sunny canopy is the busiest layer of all, while a few mobile animals (like butterflies) move between layers.

activities.title: Sort each animal into its layer
feedback: Confirm correct placements; when an animal is clearly misplaced (e.g. jaguar as a canopy resident), point back to its hook and the layer map (e.g. 'the jaguar is a ground-hunter — try the forest floor').
Treat butterflies as acceptable between/across layers, and allow that some animals use more than one layer, so a defensible placement is not marked wrong.
OPTIONAL: let a clearly wrong card spring back or glow to invite another try, so the sorting stays a game with immediate response.
activities.rationale: A drag-each-animal-to-its-layer task actively tests the naming-plus-placing goal with feedback, going beyond recognition to independent placement; it does not by itself elicit a spoken reason. Placements are typical/primary homes, so mobile species are treated flexibly. This is a proposed scaffold, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Iconic Neotropical rainforest animals (jaguars, toucans, sloths, poison dart frogs, howler monkeys, macaws, butterflies) occupy characteristic forest layers, with most animal life in the canopy
learnerActions: Given a strip or scene with the four layers marked, move each animal card to the layer where it lives (jaguar → floor; howler monkeys/toucans/macaws/sloths → canopy; dart frog → low damp understorey).
Place the butterfly card deliberately as a 'moves-between-layers' animal — it need not sit in a single layer.
Say out loud or recall the one hook for each animal as you place it (sloth = slow, howler = loudest, dart frog = tiny and bright).
activities.intendedInsight: Different animals favour different layers; placing them actively checks whether the child has connected each animal to its home rather than just naming it — while a few mobile animals (like butterflies) move between layers.

activities.title: Talk about who lives where — and why
feedback: Strong answer: the howler monkey lives up in the canopy, climbing, hanging by its tail and feeding among the treetops where there are leaves, fruit and light; the jaguar lives mainly on the forest floor, prowling and hunting on the ground.
If the child places an animal correctly but can't say why, link its body and food to its layer (monkey climbs for leaves and fruit; jaguar hunts on the ground).

If the child puts every animal on the floor or can't assign layers, revisit the layers and match tree-dwelling climbers and birds like toucans and macaws to the canopy, ground-hunters to the floor, and butterflies as moving between layers.
activities.rationale: The reason-tier surfaces whether placement is understood or guessed: a child who only names or places animals cannot necessarily explain placement by food and movement. Discussion is used to elicit that ecological link. This is a proposed scaffold, not a validated intervention.
sourceClaims: Students observe how external parts help animals survive and the diversity of life in a habitat
KS1 pupils identify, name and group animals and describe how habitats provide for them
learnerActions: Answer: a howler monkey and a jaguar both live in the rainforest, but not in the same layer — where would you find each one, and why does each live where it does?
Name another animal that lives in the canopy and one that lives on the floor.
Say one special thing about a toucan or a sloth that helps it live where it does.
Discuss: why would a monkey find it hard to live down on the dark forest floor?
activities.intendedInsight: Animals mostly live in the layer that suits how they move and where their food is — tree-climbers and leaf- and fruit-eaters up high, ground-hunters down low — so placement has a reason, not just a label.

constraints: Checkpoint tiers: name three iconic animals (age ~5); place one animal in its layer, e.g. monkeys in the canopy (age ~6); explain that different animals live in different layers with most in the canopy (age ~7).

A tap-to-reveal scene builds and checks recognition, but recognition-only responses do not show whether a child can independently place or explain; include active sorting and a spoken/written 'why' to reach the explanation tier of the goal.

Treat each layer placement as a typical/primary home, not an absolute rule: some animals use multiple layers (jaguars can climb; butterflies traverse layers), so do not mark a defensible multi-layer placement wrong.

Address misconceptions directly: most rainforest animals live in the canopy, not on the ground; animals favour particular layers rather than living everywhere; sloths are very slow and are not monkeys; poison dart frogs are tiny and their bright colour is a warning — do not teach that bright colour means safe, and do not teach touching wild frogs; jaguars mainly prowl the forest floor rather than living in trees all the time.
Keep the four-layer map from the previous topic as the shared frame so naming builds on prior layer knowledge.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; all sources[].claim were already marked verified:false in the row and have NOT been re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source describes animals occupying 'characteristic forest layers' with most life in the canopy; real animals use multiple layers and ranges overlap, so each placement is a typical/primary home rather than an absolute rule (e.g. jaguars can climb; butterflies move between layers). The sort and reveal activities now treat such multi-layer cases flexibly.
The 'most animal life in the canopy' generalisation is presented as the source states it but remains unverified; it is used as a conservative, qualified claim.

The row's 'poor fit' claim that recognition-and-placement 'doesn't need genuine 3D' was not propagated as a universal law; a 2D layered scene is proposed as sufficient and age-appropriate, without asserting 3D adds nothing in general.
Safety nuance retained: bright warning colouration signals danger, not safety; do not imply a frog is safe to handle.

probeDeeper: Name another animal that lives up in the canopy, and one that lives on the floor.
Why would a monkey find it hard to live down on the dark forest floor?
What is one special thing about a toucan or a sloth that helps it live where it does?
assess.correctAnswer: The howler monkey lives up in the canopy, swinging and feeding among the treetops where there's fruit and light; the jaguar lives down on the forest floor, prowling and hunting on the ground. Animals live in the layer that suits how they move and where their food is — tree-climbers and fruit-eaters up high, ground-hunters down low.

errorPatterns.pattern: all animals live together on the ground — no sense of layers
errorPatterns.nextMove: revisit the layers; match climbers/fliers to the canopy and ground-hunters to the floor
errorPatterns.distractor: Both live on the forest floor together
errorPatterns.revealedBy: puts every animal on the forest floor or can't assign layers

errorPatterns.pattern: animals live in a layer for no reason — misses the food-and-movement link
errorPatterns.nextMove: link each animal's body and food to its layer (monkey climbs for fruit, jaguar hunts on the ground)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: places an animal correctly but can't say why

responseLevels.gap: Names animals but can't place any in a layer, or puts them all on the ground.
responseLevels.full: Places at least three animals in the right layers and explains the placement by food and how the animal moves (canopy climbers/fliers vs floor hunters).
responseLevels.partial: Matches some animals to layers but can't explain why they live there.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A howler monkey and a jaguar both live in the rainforest, but they don't live in the same layer. Where would you find each one, and why does each animal live where it does?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who just names animals can't place them by layer; the concept child matches each animal to a layer AND gives a reason (food and movement). The reason-tier surfaces whether the placement is understood or guessed.
